- No mercy on violent crime
- More police funding
- Harsher penalties for drug dealers
- Less wars
- Skepticism of foreign intervention
- Stronger national defense
- Reduce trade dependency with China
- Return essential manufacturing to the US
- More control on illegal immigration
- Less federal oversight on education
- More parental rights for gender reassignment in minors
- More conservative interpretation of the constitution
- Stronger voting safeguards
- Less red tape at the county & city level
- Less government interference on DEI and gender issues

hits.full_text:
Pre AI your moat was tech knowledge. You learned Rails, learned to do UX better than others, and built a better product. 

2025/6 era we merged that knowledge with AI at an executional level. You have an idea for a new product or feature, you get AI to build it. Repeat. It’s 2x or 3x faster, limited by your brain and backlog. 

2027 is going to be about AI knowledge. Your framework will be a proprietary set of skills, harnesses, loops etc that do all of the strategic and executional work for you. It’s 100x faster. You check in once a day to correct course. People will try to sell toolsets like this but yours is better or more tailored for your needs.

That means most product development and technical marketing (SEO etc) is done by AI. Your job as a founder is to do the marketing stuff that AI can’t do. In person events. YouTube videos. Webinars. White glove onboarding. 

Your moat is how many X factors of speed you can get out of your AI framework, and how good your non-AI marketing is.
hits.hook: Yongfook: the moat before and after AI (~29k views, 120 replies)

hits.full_text:
Only @grok was able to help me decide how to vote in the midterms.

ChatGPT said: "I can provide factual political comparisons, but I can’t recommend a voting slate based on your personal political views."

Claude said: "Straight answer: I don’t make vote recommendations. Not for you, not for anyone, on any side. The moment I start picking candidates I’m a thumb on the scale in an election, and that’s not a role I’ll take even when asked nicely."

Gemini refused to even pull up my ballot items and said: "I cannot provide opinions on how you should vote or endorse specific candidates and measures based on your political values."

Try the same prompt yourself. You don't need to know your district number; just put your address. The grok app goes into even more depth than the reply bot on X.

@grok why are the other models refusing to answer while you have no problem doing it?
hits.hook: Vassallo: comparing chatbots on voting advice (~11k)

patterns: Quitting the journal is today's big analog thread. One line about stopping because there were only terrible things to say passed 219k views on a ~9k account, and smaller accounts are answering it with their own failed tries, including a therapist's suggestion that didn't stick.

Handwriting coming back after years away gets warm, open questions ('when did you last write something on paper?'), and analog fallbacks show up when tech fails: a 1950s typewriter, a ledger book instead of printer ink.
ADHD posts that land are funny and physical, about inertia, rolling onto the floor, and lists on receipts, rather than advice lists.
Mental health wins are concrete and dated: back at work after 11 months, a 5 km run after a year in bed.
Founder talk on the watchlist is about AI wiping out moats and ideas being built 117 times over. Yongfook alone has three posts past 14k.
Election day is pulling the watchlist toward politics (Vassallo's voting posts). Skipped for drafts.

reply_ideas.description: Kiara wrote a letter by hand for the first time in years and is asking when you last wrote something on paper
reply_ideas.reply_text: I write by hand every day, and I think handwriting comes back faster than people expect once there's a reason to use it. Who was the letter for, and did you mail it yet?

reply_ideas.description: Jasmine tried journaling when her therapist suggested it and quit after a month because it felt like documenting misery
reply_ideas.reply_text: I think a journal turns into a record of misery when every entry has to be about how you feel. Writing down one thing you actually did that day, even a walk, gives the page something else to hold. Did your therapist ever say what you were supposed to write about?

reply_ideas.description: a joke that ADHD means owning notebooks and Trello boards and still writing the to-do list on a receipt
reply_ideas.reply_text: I think the receipt wins because it's too small to become a system, so you just write the list. Do you ever go back to the notebooks, or have they turned into a museum of good intentions?

x_posts.title: Terrible things
x_posts.text:
A post saying "I stopped journalling because I only had terrible things to say" passed 200,000 views yesterday. I think a lot of people quit a notebook right around the point where it starts telling the truth.

What would you write if nobody, not even you, ever had to reread it?

x_posts.title: The receipt
x_posts.text:
Someone joked today that ADHD means owning a pile of notebooks and still writing the day's list on the back of a receipt. I think the receipt works because it's too small to turn into a whole system.

What's the strangest thing you've ever written a to-do list on?
